topic.title: Build Your Own Local AI Agent
topic.description: Local-first AI agents from the ground up: what an agent actually is, a documented how-to on Hermes Agent by Nous Research, the structural truth about hallucination, what agents can and cannot do in 2026, human-agentic orchestration patterns, and cybernetics from Wiener's 1948 definition to modern brain-computer interfaces — every claim read from its source on 2026-10-17.
topic.focus: Verified 2026-10-17 · Hermes docs, Nature 2026 hallucination paper, METR Time Horizon 1.1, Neuralink updates, UC Irvine BCI study

beginner.label: Beginner 🌱
beginner.tagline: From zero to a working local agent — every command, price and capability claim below was read from the cited source on 2026-10-17, and the through-line is verify everything.
goals: Explain an agent as model + tools + loop + memory, and name the files where a real agent keeps its state
Install and configure a local agent safely: secrets in .env, approval gates on, containers before anything destructive
Write a subagent brief a fresh-context worker can execute: objective, output format, tool guidance, boundaries
Verify instead of trust: open every citation, demand evidence, test outputs against ground truth
Read the 2026 landscape honestly: hour-scale task horizons, percent-scale hallucination, dozens of BCI trial participants

concepts.title: Module 1 — What an agent actually is
concepts.text:
A working definition: an agent is a language model plus three things — tools it can call, a loop that feeds results back to it, and memory that outlives a single message. Anthropic's engineering team defines a multi-agent system as "multiple agents (LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop) working together", and the same definition strips down to the single-agent case — [Anthropic engineering blog](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system) [V 2026-10-17].

The four parts:
- Model — the reasoning engine. At run time it knows only what is in its context; it generates the next chunk of text (tokens) and decides which tool to call next. There is no separate knowledge store being consulted
- Tools — the hands: shell/terminal, file read and write, web search and page extraction, browser control, APIs. A model without tools is a chatbot; a model with tools is a candidate agent
- Loop — the agent runs: read the request, choose a tool, run it, read the result, decide again, until done. Anthropic published the shape it teaches its research subagents explicitly as an observe-orient-decide-act loop — [Anthropic engineering blog](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system) [V 2026-10-17]
- Memory — the context window (everything the model currently sees at once) plus files that persist across sessions: notes, configuration, saved procedures ("skills") and conversation history. Memory files are how an agent keeps anything at all between runs

Two honest clarifications before anything else: an agent is a program you run, not a person, and its apparent understanding is pattern completion over its context — not knowledge of your situation. Every section that follows is downstream of taking those two facts seriously.

⚠ Verified 2026-10-17 against Nous Hermes documentation, primary research and cited sources

concepts.title: Module 2 — Why local-first: privacy, cost, sovereignty
concepts.text:
Local-first means the agent's wiring — its memory, configuration, saved skills and scheduled jobs — lives on hardware you control. Three reasons people do it, with the honest caveats:

- Privacy — the agent's memory is files on your machine and you choose what leaves it. A cloud chatbot keeps your history on someone else's servers; a self-hosted agent exposes only what you explicitly send to a model. Health, legal and financial work is the strongest case for this
- Cost — metered hosted APIs charge per token on every turn; a self-hosted model costs hardware and electricity once. But the 2026 honest answer: budget hosted tiers have collapsed to cents per full one-million-token window, so small workloads are cheaper on cheap hosted models and heavy repeated workloads are cheaper self-hosted. Do the arithmetic for your own usage instead of trusting slogans — [Third-party price tracker, October 2026](https://llmpricewatch.com/models/gemini-api-pricing-explained) [V 2026-10-17]
- Sovereignty — your skills, memory and configuration are plain files you can back up, version and move, and the model behind them is swappable. Hermes, used as the worked example below, swaps its model provider behind the same agent: Nous Portal, OpenRouter, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint including one you host yourself — [Hermes docs](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs) [V 2026-10-17]

One correction to the slogan: running on your laptop does not make an agent private if it calls a cloud model with everything it sees. Privacy comes from knowing the data path — which files the agent reads, what goes into the prompt, and where the model actually runs. Map that path before you hand the agent anything you would not paste into a public forum.

⚠ Verified 2026-10-17 against Nous Hermes documentation, primary research and cited sources

concepts.title: Module 3 — Install: Hermes Agent as the worked example
concepts.text:
Disclosure first: Hermes Agent (built by Nous Research) is the worked example here because this very module was written by a Hermes agent — apply the same skepticism to this section that you apply to everything else, and check each command against the official docs — [Official documentation](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs) [V 2026-10-17]. Hermes is one option among Claude Code, OpenAI Codex CLI and open-source frameworks; it even imports setups from the first two, which is a fair hint that no agent is irreplaceable. Source and issues are public — [GitHub repository](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent) [V 2026-10-17].

Install and first run:
- Linux, macOS, WSL2 or Android (Termux): curl -fsSL https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.sh | bash — on Windows: iex (irm https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.ps1), or use the desktop installer — [Installation guide](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/getting-started/installation) [V 2026-10-17]
- The installer brings Python 3.11 (via uv), Node.js 22, ripgrep and ffmpeg, clones the code into ~/.hermes/hermes-agent/ and symlinks the hermes command; hermes doctor diagnoses a broken install and hermes update upgrades it — [Installation guide](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/getting-started/installation) [V 2026-10-17]
- Fastest working setup: hermes setup --portal — one OAuth covers a model plus the Tool Gateway (web search, image generation, text-to-speech, cloud browser). Otherwise hermes model chooses provider and key — [Hermes docs](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs) [V 2026-10-17]

The state directory ~/.hermes/ is the whole agent: config.yaml (settings), .env (API keys), auth.json (OAuth credentials), SOUL.md (identity/personality), memories/ (MEMORY.md and USER.md), skills/ (procedural knowledge), cron/ (scheduled jobs), sessions/ and logs/ (secrets auto-redacted). Back up that directory and you have backed up the agent; delete it and you have a fresh one.

⚠ Verified 2026-10-17 against Nous Hermes documentation, primary research and cited sources

concepts.title: Module 4 — Config, gateway and security
concepts.text:
Configuration has two layers and the split matters: secrets (API keys, bot tokens) go in ~/.hermes/.env, everything else (model, terminal backend, compression, toolsets) goes in config.yaml; when both are set, config.yaml wins for non-secret settings, and settings resolve CLI arguments first, then config.yaml, then .env, then built-in defaults — [Configuration reference](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/configuration) [V 2026-10-17]. hermes config get and hermes config set route each value to the right file automatically.

Where the shell runs is a first-class setting: terminal.backend is one of local, docker, ssh, modal, daytona, vercel_sandbox or singularity — [Configuration reference](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/configuration) [V 2026-10-17]. Learn on local; move to a container before you start handing the agent destructive tools.

Gateways: Hermes connects to 19 native messaging platforms plus IRC and Microsoft Teams via plugins — Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, Matrix, email, SMS and more — one agent, many surfaces, and scheduled jobs deliver to any of them — [Hermes docs](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs) [V 2026-10-17].

Security is the part beginners skip and operators learn expensively: an agent with shell access is a person with shell access. Hermes ships command approval (confirm before dangerous commands), container isolation, an egress proxy and a credential-injection proxy, plus per-platform tool configuration — [Security model](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/security) [V 2026-10-17]. Turn the approval gate on before your first destructive experiment, not after it.

⚠ Verified 2026-10-17 against Nous Hermes documentation, primary research and cited sources

concepts.title: Module 5 — Skills: the agent's procedural memory
concepts.text:
Skills are the agent's procedural memory: documents describing how to do a task, stored in ~/.hermes/skills/ as SKILL.md files, loaded only when needed — [Skills system](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/skills) [V 2026-10-17].

- Progressive disclosure — the agent first sees only a list of names and one-line descriptions (about 3K tokens), reads a full skill on demand, then pulls specific reference files inside it. This is what makes hundreds of procedures affordable in context
- The agent writes its own skills — after it figures out a non-trivial workflow it saves it via the skill_manage tool (create, patch, write_file) and patches it later. That closed learning loop is why an agent measurably improves on task types it has seen before
- /learn teaches a new skill from a local doc directory, a URL, pasted notes, or the workflow you just demonstrated in conversation
- Open standard — skills follow the agentskills.io specification, so they are portable and shareable; third-party installs are content-hashed and quarantined with the source URL recorded — [Skills system](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/skills), [agentskills.io specification](https://agentskills.io) [V 2026-10-17]
- Trust boundaries — skills are procedures the agent follows, so project-local skills inside a cloned repo are not auto-loaded without your approval, and a skills.write_approval gate forces human sign-off on the agent's own skill writes — [Skills system](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/skills) [V 2026-10-17]

Practical rule: a skill should encode what surprised you — the pitfall, the exact command sequence, the verification step — not generic advice the model already produced correctly once.

⚠ Verified 2026-10-17 against Nous Hermes documentation, primary research and cited sources

concepts.title: Module 6 — Cron and delegation: automation and subagents
concepts.text:
Two automation layers, and the money question hides in the second one.

Scheduled jobs (cron): job definitions are plain JSON in ~/.hermes/cron/jobs.json. The gateway scheduler checks due jobs, starts a fresh agent session per run, optionally injects attached skills, runs the prompt to completion, delivers the final response to its target (Telegram, Discord, a bot chat, multiple targets) and records run metadata — [Cron jobs](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/cron) [V 2026-10-17]. Script-only mode (no_agent) runs a watchdog script with zero model calls; a [SILENT] marker suppresses delivery and [CRON_FAILURE] declares a failed run. Jobs are files, so they survive restarts and reboots.

Delegation (subagents): delegate_task spawns an isolated child agent. The critical property — a subagent starts with a completely fresh conversation: it sees only the goal and context fields its parent fills in, none of the parent's history — [Subagent delegation](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/delegation) [V 2026-10-17]. Up to 10 run concurrently by default, grouped tasks return one consolidated message, only the child's final summary enters the parent's context, and a /review command spawns an independent reviewer whose only job is to re-open and judge the work just produced.

This is where the money goes: Anthropic's published numbers say agents burn roughly 4x the tokens of a chat and multi-agent systems roughly 15x — their orchestrator-plus-subagents Research system beat a single agent by 90.2 percent on their internal research eval, and parallel tool use cut research time up to 90 percent — [Anthropic engineering blog](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system), [annotated summary](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/14/multi-agent-research-system/) [V 2026-10-17]. Parallelism buys speed and coverage; the bill scales with it.

Human-agentic rule number one, learned expensively: vague briefs produce duplicated or missing work. Every subagent brief needs an objective, an output format, tool guidance and hard task boundaries.

⚠ Verified 2026-10-17 against Nous Hermes documentation, primary research and cited sources

concepts.title: Module 7 — Hallucination: the structural problem
concepts.text:
Hallucination is not a bug to wait out — it is structural, and the 2026 literature explains exactly why.

- Cause — models are trained to predict the next token, and a 2026 Nature paper shows this creates statistical pressure toward hallucination even with error-free training data: facts that appear only once in training data (a birthday, an obscure detail) offer no pattern to learn, so the model must guess. If 20 percent of some family of facts appears exactly once, expect at least 20 percent hallucination on that family — [Nature 2026, Kalai et al](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10549-w) [V 2026-10-17]
- Incentive — evaluations are scored binary, so guessing beats admitting uncertainty. On OpenAI's SimpleQA, o4-mini answered almost everything and was wrong about 75 percent of the time, while GPT-5-mini abstained on 52 percent of questions and was wrong only 26 percent — leaderboards still reward the guesser — [OpenAI, Why language models hallucinate](https://openai.com/index/why-language-models-hallucinate/), [Nature 2026](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10549-w) [V 2026-10-17]
- Measured rates — Vectara's HHEM leaderboard (summarization, source document provided) put the best models near 2-3 percent fabrication as of September 2026 — [Vectara HHEM leaderboard](https://github.com/vectara/hallucination-leaderboard/) [V 2026-10-17] — but a 172-billion-token document Q&A study across 35 models found fabrication more than tripling as context grew, exceeding 10 percent for every model tested at 200K tokens — [RIKER study, arXiv 2603.08274](https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2603.08274) [V 2026-10-17]

The discipline that follows: treat model output as leads, never sources. Open every citation yourself — a model can fabricate a plausible title, authors and DOI in one breath. Demand tool output as evidence, not prose. When a claim matters, require two independent sources. "Verify everything" is not paranoia here; it is the correct operating manual for a system that guesses for a living.

⚠ Verified 2026-10-17 against Nous Hermes documentation, primary research and cited sources

concepts.title: Module 8 — Context, cost and model tiers in 2026
concepts.text:
Context window: how much text a model can see at once, measured in tokens (roughly three-quarters of an English word each). Third-party trackers in late 2026 list Google's Gemini 3.1 Pro at roughly one to two million tokens, Claude models at 200K stable (1M in beta) and GPT-5.x around 128K-400K — [Context window comparison, October 2026](https://morphllm.com/llm-context-window-comparison), [price tracker](https://llmpricewatch.com/models/gemini-api-pricing-explained) [V 2026-10-17].

Price per million tokens (third-party trackers, October 2026): budget tier roughly $0.10-0.50 input and $0.40-3 output; flagship tier about $2-5 input and $12-30 output; Anthropic dropped its long-context surcharge during 2026 — [price tracker](https://llmpricewatch.com/models/gemini-api-pricing-explained), [comparison table](https://morphllm.com/llm-context-window-comparison) [V 2026-10-17]. Vendor list prices move monthly: treat any figure older than a season as stale and re-check the provider's own pricing page before budgeting.

Cost structure of agents specifically: every tool result, file read and search hit enters the context and is re-sent on later turns, so the token bill grows with the work done. Prompt caching discounts the repeated prefix; compaction (summarizing old context) trades money for lost detail; delegation multiplies cost — about 15x a chat for multi-agent setups per Anthropic — [Anthropic engineering blog](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system) [V 2026-10-17].

Tier strategy: cheap fast models for mechanical steps (classification, extraction, formatting), frontier models for judgment (planning, verification, ambiguous requests). The right question is never "which model is best" but "which model clears the reliability bar for this step" — and both price and quality move, so re-measure.

⚠ Verified 2026-10-17 against Nous Hermes documentation, primary research and cited sources

concepts.title: Module 9 — What agents can and cannot do (2026)
concepts.text:
What agents actually complete, measured: nonprofit evaluator METR tracks a "time horizon" — the longest task, in human-expert completion time, that a model finishes with 50 percent success. Its Time Horizon 1.1 release (2026-01-29) found the horizon doubling about every 196 days across six years, and about every 89 days looking only at 2024 onward; published trackers of these evaluations put frontier 50-percent horizons in early-to-mid 2026 at roughly 5 hours (Claude Opus 4.5 on TH1.1) up to about 14.5 hours (Claude Opus 4.6, February 2026) — [Time Horizon 1.1 summary](https://swarchitect.net/en/loop-time-horizon-2026-09), [horizon tracker](https://singularityplus.com/agents) [V 2026-10-17].

Read that carefully: 50 percent is coin-flip. The horizon at 90 percent success is much shorter, and benchmarks are cleaner than real work — no ambiguous goals, no broken logins, no approval gates.

Reliable in 2026: file operations, code with tests the agent can actually run, web research it verifies against sources, structured transforms of text and data, and mechanical multi-step pipelines. Unreliable: exact recall of obscure facts, long unsupervised missions, judging the quality of its own output, anything physical, and knowing when it is wrong — models have no dependable internal error signal.

Design implication: verify outputs against ground truth (tests, sources, checksums), never against the agent's confidence. Confidence is free; correctness costs verification. And expect the horizon to keep growing — the doubling is real — but re-run your own acceptance tests when you upgrade the model, because capability updates silently change behavior.

⚠ Verified 2026-10-17 against Nous Hermes documentation, primary research and cited sources

concepts.title: Module 10 — Human-agentic systems: operating patterns
concepts.text:
Orchestrating humans and agents together as one system. These patterns come from Anthropic's published multi-agent engineering lessons and from operating real agent fleets; where the second is the source, it is labeled as operator experience — [Anthropic engineering blog](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system) [V 2026-10-17].

- Orchestrator plus worker lanes — one lead agent plans and delegates while specialized subagents explore in parallel, each with its own context window. Anthropic's Research system is exactly this, including a dedicated citation-checking agent that runs before the answer is returned
- Plan-doc-first — write the plan to a file before executing anything. Anthropic's lead agent saves its plan to memory because a 200K-token context can be truncated mid-mission; the plan must outlive the window. A plan on disk is also reviewable by a human and by an independent reviewer agent
- Verification gates — separate generation from judgment: an independent reviewer that re-opens the artifacts rather than trusting the transcript, citation passes that check every link resolves, and tests as acceptance criteria. Anthropic reports small eval sets (20-30 queries) exposing 30-80 percent effect sizes from prompt changes — cheap insurance
- Approval scoping — humans keep the irreversible steps: command approval gates, least-privilege credentials, network egress controls. Subagents inherit the parent's provider credentials, so scope what a child can reach before spawning it — [Subagent delegation](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/delegation), [Security model](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/security) [V 2026-10-17]
- Effort scaling — fact-finding is one agent with a handful of tool calls; a direct comparison is a few subagents; complex research is 10+ with hard divisions of labor. Under-scoping wastes hours on duplicated work; over-scoping burns money for nothing

Fleet lessons, honestly labeled as operator experience: coordination failures are mostly briefing failures; only final summaries should enter the orchestrator's context; watch the roster while it runs instead of trusting it silently; and keep a human on the approval rail for anything that spends money, sends messages or deletes data.

⚠ Verified 2026-10-17 against Nous Hermes documentation, primary research and cited sources

concepts.title: Module 11 — Cybernetics: Wiener to brain-computer interfaces
concepts.text:
The actual definition: cybernetics is Norbert Wiener's term, from the Greek kybernetes (steersman; the same root as "governor"), and it is defined by the subtitle of his 1948 book — Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine — [Wiley, Cybernetics encyclopedia entry](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/9780470050118.ecse930), [Cybernetics (book)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cybernetics:_Or_Control_and_Communication_in_the_Animal_and_the_Machine) [V 2026-10-17]. Its organizing idea is feedback-mediated regulation: a system senses its own state, compares it to a goal, and acts on the difference (the error signal). A thermostat, a nervous reflex and an LLM agent are all in scope — not because they share a substance, but because they share the formal problem of acting under delay, noise and partial information.

That framing explains today's agent better than the marketing does: tools are sensors and actuators, the model is the controller, the goal is the setpoint — and a hallucination is bad telemetry. Wiener's own warning, echoed in his later book The Human Use of Human Beings, was that systems fail not only from lack of power but from bad signals and false images of their own condition, and he raised social concerns about automation that read as current.

Where cybernetics is literal — brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), state of the art in 2026:
- Neuralink's Telepathy: 21 trial participants announced January 28 2026 — [Neuralink, Two Years of Telepathy](https://neuralink.com/updates/two-years-of-telepathy/) [V 2026-10-17]; its PRIME study (NCT06429735) is a first-in-human feasibility study of the N1 implant in people with tetraplegia or tetraparesis, with 15 estimated enrollment — [ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06429735](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06429735) [V 2026-10-17]; an October 2026 Neuralink update reported an 11.32 bits-per-second decoding record and 50,000 hours of brain data — [Neuralink update](https://neuralink.com/updates/pretraining-on-50000-hours/) [V 2026-10-17]. For scale, an able-bodied mouse user manages roughly 8-10 bits per second
- Bidirectional BCIs (motor commands out, sensation back): a UC Irvine-led team with Caltech and Keck School of Medicine of USC published a brain-controlled exoskeleton system (Brain Stimulation, April 2026) that decoded stepping intent at 0.92 correlation and stimulated the sensory cortex so a paralyzed participant felt her steps, scoring 93 percent on a blind step-counting task, using the FDA-approved Ekso GT exoskeleton — [UC Irvine release](https://news.uci.edu/2026/04/16/uc-irvine-led-study-achieves-brain-controlled-walking-with-artificial-sensory-feedback), [study summary](https://insidebci.com/research/2026-04-16-bidirectional-brain-computer-interface-restores-sensation-during-brain-controlled-walking) [V 2026-10-17]

Hype check in both directions: implanted BCIs in 2026 number in the dozens of trial participants worldwide, for severe paralysis — not consumer mind-reading, and no consumer device exists; meanwhile the much-advertised "human-AI merger" today means keyboards, APIs and software agents — the loop that has actually closed between humans and machines is Wiener's feedback loop, with the human keeping the setpoint.

⚠ Verified 2026-10-17 against Nous Hermes documentation, primary research and cited sources

examples.title: Scenario A — the confident fake citation
examples.scenario: A researcher asks a local agent for sources on a narrow topic. The agent returns four citations with plausible authors, journals and years, and a fluent summary. Three of the four papers do not exist.
examples.outcome: Every citation was a lead, not a source. The fix is discipline, not a different model: open each link yourself, confirm it resolves to the document described, and require the agent to show the tool output it based the summary on. Systems that force evidence into the loop — a citation-checking pass, an independent reviewer that re-opens the artifacts — catch this structurally instead of hopefully.

examples.title: Scenario B — the vague delegation
examples.scenario: A lead agent delegates "Fix the error in the dashboard" to a subagent. The subagent, which has never seen the conversation, guesses at three different errors, edits two files, and returns a confused summary.
examples.outcome: Subagents start with a completely fresh conversation. The brief needed the goal, the exact file and line, the observed error text, the environment, and the definition of done. Anthropic found the same failure in production: without an objective, output format, tool guidance and task boundaries, subagents duplicate work or leave gaps.

examples.title: Scenario C — the long-context trap
examples.scenario: A support workflow keeps one long agent conversation open all week. By Friday, answers that used to be right drift: the agent mixes up two tickets and invents a policy clause that does not exist.
examples.outcome: Fabrication rises with context length: the 172-billion-token study found rates exceeding 10 percent for every model tested at 200K tokens, even though the best were near 1 percent at 32K — long context is not free recall. Fix: keep durable state in written records instead of chat history, re-ground each session from source files, and start a fresh session per ticket.

pitfalls: MYTH: “The agent remembers our conversations.” Context is per-session; without persistent memory files, every fresh session starts blank — and subagents always start blank, seeing only the goal and context their parent provides.
MYTH: “Running it locally makes it private.” Only if the model itself runs on your machine; a local shell agent pointed at a cloud API still sends everything it sees to the vendor. Map the data path.
A citation in model output is a lead, not a source — open it yourself before you repeat it to anyone.
Bigger context does not mean better recall: fabrication more than tripled as context grew in the 172-billion-token document Q&A study, exceeding 10 percent at 200K tokens for every model tested.
Multi-agent setups use about 15x the tokens of a chat (Anthropic's own numbers) — buy parallelism only where the task's value pays for it.
An agent with shell access is a person with shell access — command approval gates and least-privilege credentials belong on before the first destructive command, not after.
A 50 percent task horizon (METR) is coin-flip reliability; the horizon at 90 percent success is much shorter, and benchmark tasks are cleaner than real work.
Model upgrades silently change behavior — pin versions where you can, and re-run your acceptance checklist after any model or tool change.
exercises: Install a local agent (Hermes or any alternative) on a machine you can afford to experiment on. Write down where each of these lives: settings, secrets, memory, scheduled jobs, saved procedures. If you cannot answer for your own tool, you do not yet know its data path.

Pick one task you would trust an agent to do weekly. Write the verification checklist a human would need before accepting its output — the ground truth for every claim it will produce. That checklist is your acceptance test.

Run the same research question once through a single agent and once through an orchestrator with parallel subagents. Compare not just the answers but token usage and wall-clock time, then decide with numbers whether 15x the tokens bought enough quality for your use case.

glossary.definition: A language model wired to tools and run in a loop, with memory that outlives a single message. Model plus tools plus loop plus memory.
How much text (in tokens) a model can see at once; everything sent to it is re-sent on later turns until compacted or evicted.
The unit text is split into for a model, roughly three-quarters of an English word; both pricing and context limits are counted in tokens.
A confident, plausible falsehood. Structurally unavoidable for one-off facts under next-token training, and rewarded by binary-scored evaluations that prefer guessing to abstention.
A saved procedure document the agent loads on demand — procedural memory, written by a human or by the agent, stored in ~/.hermes/skills/ and following the agentskills.io standard.
The lead agent that plans, decomposes work and delegates to subagents; it should keep only final summaries in its context and the plan on disk.
An isolated child agent spawned by delegate_task with a completely fresh conversation — it sees only the goal and context fields its parent fills in.
A separate step that checks outputs against ground truth — tests, sources, checksums — instead of against the agent's confidence.
Norbert Wiener's 1948 field: control and communication in the animal and the machine, organized around feedback loops, error signals and noise.
Brain-computer interface: electrodes that read motor intent and, in bidirectional systems, stimulate the sensory cortex to return sensation. 2026 trials involve dozens of participants worldwide.

beginner.q: In the working definition used in this module, what turns a language model into an agent?
options: Fine-tuning it on your own documents
A bigger context window than a chatbot has
Running on local hardware instead of the cloud
Tools it can call, a loop that feeds results back, and memory that outlives one message
beginner.explain: The definition is model plus tools plus loop plus memory. Bigger windows, local hardware and fine-tuning change the economics or the quality, but none of them creates the loop that makes an agent.

beginner.q: In Hermes Agent, where do API keys and bot tokens belong?
options: auth.json only
config.yaml, which wins over everything
~/.hermes/.env — secrets live in .env, everything else in config.yaml
SOUL.md so the agent remembers them
beginner.explain: Secrets go in .env and everything else in config.yaml; when both are set, config.yaml wins for non-secret settings. Resolution order is CLI arguments, then config.yaml, then .env, then built-in defaults.

beginner.q: A parent agent calls delegate_task with the goal “Fix the error.” What does the subagent see?
options: Only the goal and context fields the parent fills in — subagents start with a completely fresh conversation
Nothing at all until the parent sends a follow-up message
The parent's full conversation history
The parent's memory files but not its chat
beginner.explain: Subagents have zero knowledge of the parent's history or prior tool calls. Their only context is the goal and context the parent provides, which is why vague briefs produce duplicated or missing work.

beginner.q: According to the 2026 Nature paper cited here, why do language models hallucinate?
options: Models deliberately deceive users
Next-token training cannot learn facts that appear only once, and binary-scored evaluations reward guessing over admitting uncertainty
Context windows truncate mid-answer
Training data contains too many errors
beginner.explain: The paper shows the statistical pressure exists even with error-free data (one-off facts have no pattern to learn), then argues hallucination persists because accuracy metrics penalize abstention: a model that guesses outscores one that admits uncertainty.

beginner.q: What does Vectara's HHEM leaderboard actually measure?
options: Overall factual accuracy on open questions
How often a model refuses to answer
Speed of token generation
How often a model fabricates content when summarizing a document, judged against that document
beginner.explain: HHEM scores summarization factual consistency with the source document provided — an analogue for truthfulness, not a general truth test. As of September 2026 the best models sit near 2-3 percent fabrication on that task.

beginner.q: Per Anthropic's published numbers, roughly how many tokens does a multi-agent system use compared with a chat?
options: About 100x
About the same
About 15x
About 2x
beginner.explain: Anthropic reports agents use about 4x the tokens of a chat and multi-agent systems about 15x. That system beat a single agent by 90.2 percent on their internal research eval — performance bought, in part, with tokens.

beginner.q: What does Norbert Wiener's 1948 book subtitle define cybernetics as?
options: Control and communication in the animal and the machine
Artificial intelligence before it had a name
The mathematics of information transmission alone
The study of thinking machines
beginner.explain: Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine. The term comes from the Greek kybernetes (steersman), and the field is organized around feedback-mediated regulation in organisms and machines alike.

options: The doubling time of GPU performance
How long a model can keep running before it degrades
The longest task, in human-expert completion time, that a model completes with 50 percent success
Wall-clock execution time on benchmark tasks
beginner.explain: It is a difficulty measure in human-time units at coin-flip success, not a runtime. Time Horizon 1.1 (January 2026) put the frontier at roughly 5 to 14.5 hours depending on model and eval date, doubling about every 196 days overall and about every 89 days since 2024.

beginner.q: A larger context window means the model will not fabricate — the 172-billion-token study found fabrication rates fell as context grew.
beginner.explain: The opposite held: fabrication more than tripled as context grew, exceeding 10 percent for every model tested at 200K tokens, even though the best sat near 1 percent at 32K. Long context is not free recall.

beginner.q: Cybernetics comes from the Greek word for steersman, and Wiener's field covered feedback regulation in both organisms and machines.
beginner.explain: From kybernetes (steersman; the same root as governor), defined by the subtitle of Wiener's 1948 book. Its core is feedback-mediated regulation — sense state, compare to goal, act on the difference — across animals, machines and organizations.
